parts.context: Two staff members at a provincial park are discussing a problem at the campground just before a long weekend.

lines: Tobias, have you got a minute before you head out on patrol? The conservation officer just called me back about the bear in Loop C.
Is this the young male that’s been hanging around the garbage enclosure? I saw him behind the comfort station on Sunday, just strolling along like he owned the place.

Same one, she thinks. Last night it got into a cooler at site forty-one. The campers had gone into town for dinner and left everything sitting on the picnic table. By the time they got back, there were wrappers scattered halfway down to the lake.
Well, that’s exactly what we tell people not to do. But nobody got hurt?

No, thank goodness. The problem is what happens next. She said once a bear connects campsites with food, it gets bolder every single time. If it gets another couple of easy meals, she won’t have much choice. It won’t be relocated; it’ll be put down.
That would be awful. Can’t she just trap it and move it up north somewhere?

She can’t set a trap until Tuesday at the earliest, and she said relocation rarely works with bears that are already used to human food. They tend to walk straight back. And here’s the timing problem: it’s the long weekend. Loop C is fully booked, sixty-four sites, and most people arrive Friday afternoon.
Right. So what if we just put up extra warning signs and hand out the bear-safety flyer at the gate? People will read it if the staff make a real point of it.
Honestly? We already hand that flyer to every single car that comes through, and we still found a cooler on a picnic table last night. I don’t think paper is going to save this bear.

qs.q: What happened at site forty-one last night?
o: A bear entered a tent while the campers were asleep.
Campers left their cooler beside the garbage enclosure.
A bear helped itself to food that was left unattended.
Campers chased a bear away from their picnic table.
qs.ev: The campers had gone into town for dinner and left everything sitting on the picnic table
qs.x: The campers were in town and the food was on the table, so the bear ate food nobody was watching. The garbage enclosure is where Tobias saw the bear earlier, not where the cooler was.

qs.q: According to the conservation officer, what will probably happen if the bear keeps finding food?
o: Officials will likely have to destroy the animal.
The bear will be trapped and moved farther north.
The bear will gradually become afraid of people.
Loop C will be closed for the rest of the season.
qs.ev: It won’t be relocated; it’ll be put down
qs.x: “Put down” means killed, so the animal would be destroyed. Moving it north is Tobias’s suggestion, which the officer says rarely works with food-conditioned bears.

qs.q: What does Gwen think of Tobias’s suggestion about signs and flyers?
o: It would cost too much to print enough of them for everyone.
It could work if staff explain the rules carefully.
It is a sensible first step before calling the officer.
It depends on a method that has already proved inadequate.
qs.ev: I don’t think paper is going to save this bear
qs.x: The flyer is already given to every car and a cooler was still left out, so she doubts it will work. Tobias, not Gwen, believes it could work if staff make a point of it.

lines: Okay, fair point. Then the obvious option is to close Loop C completely until the officer has dealt with the bear.

I thought about that, and I raised it with the superintendent this morning. She said she’d support a closure if it came to that, but she’d really rather not cancel sixty-four bookings two days before a holiday. We’d be refunding more than eleven thousand dollars, and every one of those families would suddenly have nowhere to go.
Could we move them all into Loop A instead? It’s just on the other side of the river.
Loop A only has twenty open sites this weekend. The rest are reserved, and we can’t bump people who booked months ago. So that would cover maybe a third of them at best.
Hmm. What about those bear-proof food lockers we put in at the backcountry sites? Didn’t facilities order extra ones last year?

There are twelve in the maintenance yard, still in their boxes. But twelve lockers for sixty-four sites doesn’t really solve anything. Mind you, it gave me an idea. Every incident this spring has been at a tent site, not at a trailer. People in trailers and RVs can lock their food inside, and the bear can’t get at it.
So you’re thinking we don’t close the loop, we just restrict who can camp in it?
Exactly. Hard-sided units only in Loop C. I checked the bookings, and twenty-two of the sixty-four are tents. If we move those twenty-two into Loop A, we’re only two sites short.
And the two extra could go in the overflow area by the boat launch. It’s not glamorous, but it’s flat and it’s close to the washrooms.
That works. Nobody gets cancelled, and the bear finds a lot less to interest it.

qs.q: What did the superintendent say about closing Loop C?
o: She refused because the refunds would cost too much.
She would accept it but sees it as a last resort.
She wanted the conservation officer to decide first.
She asked Gwen to wait until after the holiday.
qs.ev: She said she’d support a closure if it came to that
qs.x: “If it came to that” and “she’d rather not” show she would allow a closure only if nothing else worked. She did not refuse; the refund figure is Gwen’s worry, not a refusal.

qs.q: Why does Gwen mention trailers and RVs?
o: They can be moved to the backcountry sites more easily.
Their owners were the ones who left food out last night.
They are where the twelve food lockers will be installed.
Campers using them can keep food secure from the bear.
qs.ev: People in trailers and RVs can lock their food inside
qs.x: Hard-sided units let campers store food out of the bear’s reach, which is why only they will stay in Loop C. The lockers are for the backcountry, and the cooler was at a tent site.

qs.q: Where will the tent campers who do not fit into Loop A stay?
o: On a level area near where boats are launched
At backcountry sites that have food lockers
In Loop C, beside the trailers and RVs
In reserved sites that Loop A will free up
qs.ev: the two extra could go in the overflow area by the boat launch
qs.x: The two extra sites go in the flat overflow area by the boat launch. Reserved Loop A sites cannot be used because staff “can’t bump people who booked months ago”.

lines: But I don’t think moving the tents is enough on its own. If the bear wanders through Loop C on Saturday and finds a greasy barbecue or a bag of garbage left by a picnic table, we’re right back where we started.
Agreed. What if I do an extra patrol through Loop C on Friday and Saturday evenings? Say from eight until eleven. I can remind people to clean up and lock everything away before dark.
I appreciate the offer, but you’re on the six a.m. shift all weekend. I’d rather ask the two summer students. They’re both trained, and they’ve been asking for more hours anyway.
Fair enough. And the twelve lockers?
Let’s put them at the Loop A sites where the tent campers are going. Those people won’t know the area, and they’ll be closer to the river, where the bear has been travelling.
Makes sense. I’ll get facilities to bolt them down on Thursday. Then I’ll email the twenty-two tent campers first thing tomorrow to tell them about their new sites.

Could you do that this afternoon instead? A lot of families leave on Thursday night to beat the traffic, and some of them won’t check email once they’re on the road. And if anyone hasn’t replied by noon tomorrow, give them a call.
Will do. What are you going to tell the officer?
I’m going to ask whether she can bring the trap out on Saturday instead of Tuesday, just in case. And I’ll let the superintendent know we’ve avoided a closure, at least for now.

qs.q: Why does Gwen think moving the tent campers is not enough?
o: The trailer owners have already complained about the bear.
The overflow area is too close to the river.
Food smells left in Loop C could still attract the bear.
The summer students have not been trained to patrol.
qs.ev: finds a greasy barbecue or a bag of garbage left by a picnic table
qs.x: She worries that leftover food or garbage in Loop C would still draw the bear back. The river is mentioned only in relation to Loop A, and the students are described as trained.

qs.q: What will Tobias most likely do this afternoon?
o: Carry out an evening patrol of Loop C
Contact the campers who have to change sites
Ask facilities to install the food lockers
Phone the conservation officer about the trap
qs.ev: Could you do that this afternoon instead?
qs.x: Gwen asks him to email the twenty-two tent campers this afternoon rather than tomorrow, and he agrees. The patrol was given to the students, and Gwen will call the officer herself.

parts.context: Two neighbours are talking over the fence about a new home heating system.

lines: Colleen, I’ve been meaning to ask you. Is that the heat pump everyone on the street keeps talking about? The big grey box beside your driveway?
That’s the one. It went in at the end of October, so I’ve had it through one full winter now.
And? Simran keeps telling me they don’t work when it gets really cold. She’s convinced we’d freeze.

Well, she’s not completely wrong about the older models. But this is one of the cold-climate ones. It ran on its own down to about minus twenty-five. Below that, the old gas furnace kicks in automatically. I decided to keep it as a backup rather than have it taken out, and I think we needed it maybe six or seven nights all winter.
Huh. And the installation? I’ve heard some horror stories.

I got three quotes. The first company was the cheapest, but the salesman never bothered to work out how much heat the house actually loses. He just looked at the square footage and picked a unit. The second company spent two hours measuring everything, checking the attic, the windows, all of it. I went with them.
What about noise? That’s Simran’s other worry. Our bedroom faces your side.
You tell me. Have you heard it?
Now that you mention it, no. Not once.
There you go. It hums a bit when it’s working hard, but honestly, my dishwasher makes more racket.
Okay, but the real question is money. Is it saving you anything?

It’s a bit complicated. My gas bill went from about a hundred and eighty a month in winter to around eighty-five. But the electricity bill went up by roughly sixty. So it’s a saving, just not the dramatic one the brochure promised.
Still, that adds up over a few years.

It does. But if I could do it again, I’d do one thing differently. The installer told me my attic insulation was pretty thin. If I’d topped it up first, I probably could have bought a smaller unit and saved a couple of thousand. So if you’re serious, I’d get a proper energy assessment done before you even call anyone for quotes.
That makes sense. Simran will like that, actually. She always wants to do things in the right order.
I’ll text you the name of the company that did my assessment tonight.

qs.q: Why did Colleen not hire the first company?
o: Its price was higher than the other two quotes.
It could not install the unit until the following spring.
It wanted to remove her old gas furnace.
It chose a unit without assessing the house properly.
qs.ev: the salesman never bothered to work out how much heat the house actually loses
qs.x: The salesman picked a unit from the square footage alone, without checking heat loss. The first company was actually the cheapest, so the price option reverses what she said.

qs.q: What did Colleen decide to do with her old furnace?
o: Leave it in place for extremely cold weather
Have it removed after the first winter
Replace it with a smaller gas model
Use it whenever the heat pump is noisy
qs.ev: I decided to keep it as a backup rather than have it taken out
qs.x: She kept the furnace as a backup that starts below about minus twenty-five. A “smaller unit” refers to the heat pump she could have bought, not a new furnace.

qs.q: What is Colleen suggesting when she asks Harjit whether he has heard the unit?
o: Harjit should tell her if the noise bothers him.
The unit has been moved away from his bedroom.
His wife’s worry about noise is probably unfounded.
The unit is switched off during most nights.
qs.ev: my dishwasher makes more racket
qs.x: Her question makes Harjit realize he has never heard it, implying Simran’s worry is unnecessary. Nothing is said about moving the unit or switching it off at night.

qs.q: Overall, how has Colleen’s monthly energy cost changed in winter?
o: It has dropped by about $95.
It has dropped by about $35.
It has risen by about $60.
It has stayed roughly the same.
qs.ev: the electricity bill went up by roughly sixty
qs.x: Gas fell by about $95 ($180 to $85), but electricity rose by about $60, so the net saving is roughly $35. The $95 figure ignores the higher electricity bill.

qs.q: What will Harjit most likely do first?
o: Arrange for an expert to evaluate his home’s energy use
Get a quote from the company that Colleen hired
Add more insulation to his attic by himself this weekend
Ask Simran to come and listen to Colleen’s unit
qs.ev: I’d get a proper energy assessment done before you even call anyone for quotes
qs.x: Colleen advises an energy assessment before any quotes, Harjit agrees, and she will send him the assessor’s name. Getting quotes comes later in the order she recommends.

parts.context: A resident calls his city’s water utility about summer watering rules.

lines: Good morning, Westbrook Water Services, Mireille speaking.
Hi, yes. I found a notice stuck to my door this morning from a bylaw officer. Apparently my sprinkler was on at the wrong time last night? I honestly thought I was following the rules.

I’m sorry about that. Let me explain how it works this summer, because the rules did change in June. We’re at Stage Two restrictions now. Lawns can be watered only one morning a week, between four and nine a.m. Houses with even numbers water on Wednesdays, odd numbers on Saturdays.
Only mornings? Last year we could do it in the evening too.
That’s right, the evening window was dropped this year. Watering in the early morning loses much less to evaporation. Can I ask what your address is?

So an even number, Wednesday mornings. And just so you know, the notice you received is a warning. There’s no fine for a first time. But if it happens again, it’s a two-hundred-and-fifty-dollar penalty.
Okay, good to know. The thing is, I laid new sod in the back yard ten days ago, and the landscaper told me it has to be watered every day for the first few weeks or it’ll die.

He’s right about that, and we have a new-lawn permit for exactly that situation. It’s free, and it lets you water daily, but only for twenty-one days from the date the sod went down, not from the date you apply. You’d need to apply online and keep the permit visible in a front window.
Better than nothing, I suppose. What about my vegetable garden? The tomatoes are looking pretty sad.

Gardens are treated differently. You can water vegetables, flowers and shrubs any day, at any time, as long as you do it by hand, with a watering can or a hose that has a shut-off nozzle. Sprinklers and soaker hoses still have to follow the lawn schedule.
Oh, that’s helpful. And I saw something about rain barrels on your website?

Yes, we sell them for forty dollars each, with a maximum of two per household. The next sale is on August ninth. Orders have to be placed online by August first, and you pick them up at the public works yard on Fuller Road between eight and noon. We don’t deliver, I’m afraid.
And do you think these restrictions will be lifted any time soon? It’s been so dry.
Well, that depends on the reservoir levels and the weather, and they’re reviewed every two weeks. But between you and me, with the forecasts we’ve been seeing, I wouldn’t count on it before the fall.
Okay. Thanks, Mireille, this has been really useful.

qs.q: Why did Anwar receive a notice?
o: He watered his lawn on the wrong day of the week.
He ran his sprinkler during hours no longer allowed.
He did not display his new-lawn permit in a window.
He used a garden hose without a shut-off nozzle.
qs.ev: the evening window was dropped this year
qs.x: His sprinkler ran in the evening, which is no longer permitted; only 4–9 a.m. is allowed. Nothing suggests the day was wrong, and he has not yet applied for a permit.

qs.q: How many more days of daily watering could Anwar’s new lawn receive under the permit?
o: Ten
Twenty-one
Thirty-one
Eleven
qs.ev: only for twenty-one days from the date the sod went down
qs.x: The 21 days start when the sod was laid, ten days ago, so about eleven remain. Twenty-one would be correct only if the count started on the application date.

qs.q: What is true about watering Anwar’s vegetable garden?
o: It is allowed daily if done by hand with suitable equipment.
It may be done only on Wednesdays between four and nine.
It requires the same permit as the new sod in the back yard.
It may be done with soaker hoses at any time of the day.
qs.ev: as long as you do it by hand, with a watering can or a hose that has a shut-off nozzle
qs.x: Gardens can be watered any day by hand with a can or a nozzle hose. Soaker hoses must follow the lawn schedule, so that option reverses the rule.

qs.q: What would happen if Anwar breaks the watering rules again?
o: He would receive a second written warning.
His new-lawn permit would be cancelled.
He would be charged a fine.
His water supply would be reduced.
qs.ev: if it happens again, it’s a two-hundred-and-fifty-dollar penalty
qs.x: A second offence brings a $250 penalty, which is a fine. The warning was only for the first time, and nothing is said about cancelling permits or reducing supply.

qs.q: What must a resident do to get rain barrels?
o: Pay forty dollars when they are delivered
Order up to two of them by telephone
Pick them up at the yard on August first
Order in advance and collect them in person
qs.ev: Orders have to be placed online by August first
qs.x: Residents order online by August 1 and pick the barrels up at the works yard; there is no delivery. August 1 is the ordering deadline, not the pickup date, which is August 9.

qs.q: What does Mireille imply about the watering restrictions?
o: They will probably be relaxed at the next review.
They are likely to stay in place for the rest of summer.
They depend mainly on how carefully residents follow them.
They will become stricter if the reservoir drops.
qs.ev: I wouldn’t count on it before the fall
qs.x: Her personal comment suggests the rules will last until autumn. Reviews happen every two weeks, but she hints they are unlikely to change; she never says they will become stricter.

parts.context: You will hear a news report about wildfire smoke affecting a city.

lines: Smoke from wildfires burning more than four hundred kilometres to the north has settled over Port Albion for a third straight day, and health officials say conditions are likely to get worse before they get better. The Air Quality Health Index reached nine this morning, and forecasters expect it to climb above ten, the highest-risk category, by Thursday afternoon. In response, the Port Albion District School Board has moved all recess and physical education classes indoors for the rest of the week. Friday’s regional track and field meet, which was expected to draw more than six hundred students, has been postponed until June twelfth. The city has also extended hours at all five public library branches, which will stay open until nine p.m. as clean-air spaces for residents who don’t have air filtration at home. The region’s medical officer of health, Dr. Felix Brandt, says the smoke is a concern for everyone, but particularly for young children, older adults and people with heart or lung conditions.

The fine particles in wildfire smoke go deep into the lungs and can even enter the bloodstream. Our general advice is to keep windows closed and limit time outdoors. But I want to add a caution. It’s going to be thirty-one degrees on Thursday. If you don’t have air conditioning, sealing yourself inside a hot apartment can actually be more dangerous than the smoke. In that case, go to a library or another cooled, filtered space for a few hours.

Dr. Brandt also addressed the question of masks. He said cloth and standard surgical masks offer little protection against smoke particles, while a well-fitted N95 respirator can filter out most of them. He cautioned that the masks need a proper seal, which is difficult to achieve for people with beards and for young children. Forecasters expect a change in wind direction on Sunday to push the smoke east, out over the lake. But Dr. Brandt warned residents not to treat that as the end of the problem.

We’re only in early June. Fire seasons are getting longer, and I’d encourage people to use the clear days ahead to buy a portable air cleaner or set one up, before stores run out again like they did last year.

qs.q: What is the report mainly about?
o: How local institutions are responding to poor air quality
What caused the fires burning in the north of the province
A plan to move vulnerable residents out of Port Albion
New filtration equipment bought for the city’s libraries
qs.ev: In response, the Port Albion District School Board has moved all recess and physical education classes indoors
qs.x: The report covers how schools, libraries and health officials are reacting to the smoke. The fires’ causes are never discussed, and libraries got longer hours, not new equipment.

qs.q: What has happened to the track and field meet?
o: It has been moved to an indoor venue.
It has been limited to six hundred students.
It will take place later in the month.
It has been cancelled for this year.
qs.ev: has been postponed until June twelfth
qs.x: Postponed to June 12, in early June, means it will happen later that month. Six hundred is the expected attendance, not a limit, and only recess and gym classes moved indoors.

qs.q: Why does Dr. Brandt add a caution about staying indoors?
o: Indoor air is usually more polluted than outdoor air.
Extreme heat inside a home can pose a greater risk.
Most libraries do not have enough air filtration.
Closed windows trap the smoke particles inside.
qs.ev: sealing yourself inside a hot apartment can actually be more dangerous than the smoke
qs.x: With 31 degrees forecast, a closed-up apartment without air conditioning may be more dangerous than the smoke. He recommends libraries as filtered spaces, so the filtration option contradicts him.

qs.q: What does Dr. Brandt say about masks?
o: Surgical masks work well if they are worn correctly.
Children should wear N95 masks whenever outdoors.
Cloth masks are acceptable for short periods outside.
N95 masks are effective only when tightly fitted.
qs.ev: the masks need a proper seal
qs.x: A “well-fitted” N95 with a “proper seal” filters most particles. He says a seal is hard for young children, so recommending N95s for children misreads him.

qs.q: What does Dr. Brandt suggest about the coming weeks?
o: The smoke will clear for good on Sunday.
Air cleaners will be easy to find this year.
Residents should expect more smoky periods.
Schools will stay closed until the autumn.
qs.ev: Fire seasons are getting longer
qs.x: He warns that the wind change is not the end and urges people to prepare during clear days, so more smoke is likely. He hints stores may run out, which contradicts the air-cleaner option.

parts.context: Three members of a community garden committee are deciding how to spend a grant.

lines: Okay, last item. The neighbourhood fund confirmed our grant: six thousand dollars, and it has to be spent by the end of October. I’ve collected three proposals, so let’s hear the case for each. Kwame, do you want to start?

Sure. Mine’s the drip irrigation system. As you all know, the city capped our water allowance this summer, and we went over it twice in July. That cost us almost four hundred dollars in surcharges. A drip system with timers puts the water right at the roots, so we’d probably use about half of what we use now. The full quote is forty-eight hundred, installed.

That’s nearly the whole grant, though. My proposal is four raised, wheelchair-height beds near the gate. We lost two of our longest-serving members this year, Mrs. Petrov and Arthur, because they simply couldn’t kneel anymore. And there are three people on the waiting list who use mobility aids. The beds are thirty-five hundred for all four.

And mine, which I’ll admit is the least exciting, is a lockable shed. We’ve had tools disappear three times since May, and people are bringing their own from home and leaving them lying around in the plots, which is a bit of a mess. A shed runs about twenty-two hundred.

I hear you on the tools, Marguerite, but honestly, a padlocked storage box would do the same job for a fraction of the price. The water problem isn’t going away. If next summer is as dry as this one, the city could cut us off entirely.
Could they really? I thought the cap was a one-time thing.
The letter said they’d review the allocation for high users. I read that as a warning.
Maybe. But I’d point out that irrigation helps plants, and the beds help people. A garden that only able-bodied gardeners can use isn’t really a community garden.
That’s a bit unfair. Water affects every single plot, including the accessible ones. I’m not against the beds.
Okay, okay. Let’s look at the numbers. Ingrid’s beds plus Kwame’s full system would be eighty-three hundred. We can’t do both as quoted.

Not as quoted, no. But the installer did give me a second option: soaker hoses on timers instead of the full drip setup. Less precise, but it would still cut our use by maybe a third. That one’s nineteen hundred.
Then the beds and the soaker hoses together come to fifty-four hundred. That leaves six hundred.
Which, I suppose, would cover a decent storage box and a couple of good locks. Fine. I’ll let the shed go, for this year at least.

I’m not going to pretend soaker hoses are what I wanted. But if it keeps us under the cap, I can live with it. On one condition: we start collecting rainwater from the community centre roof next spring.
I’d support that. And we could apply to the same fund again in January to pay for the barrels.

Alright, so it’s the four raised beds, the soaker hose system, and a lockable box with whatever’s left. Ingrid, can you contact the people on the waiting list and find out if they still want plots? Kwame, you’ll book the installer?
I’ll call him tomorrow. He told me he’s fully booked until mid-September, so the sooner the better.
And I’ll draft something for the newsletter so members know where the money went. People always ask.

qs.q: Why does Kwame support the drip irrigation system?
o: The city has offered to pay part of the installation.
Many plants died during the dry weeks in July.
The garden’s current hoses are leaking badly.
The garden has paid penalties for exceeding a limit.
qs.ev: That cost us almost four hundred dollars in surcharges
qs.x: Going over the water cap twice led to surcharges, which are penalties. July is when the garden exceeded the cap; he never says plants died.

qs.q: Why did two long-time members leave the garden?
o: They were frustrated by the long waiting list.
They could no longer garden at ground level.
Their tools kept disappearing from their plots.
They moved to plots with better irrigation.
qs.ev: they simply couldn’t kneel anymore
qs.x: Being unable to kneel means they could not work in ground-level plots. The waiting list holds new applicants with mobility aids; it was not why members left.

qs.q: How does Marguerite present her own proposal?
o: She admits it is the least appealing of the three.
She insists it is the most urgent of the three.
She says it would save the most money overall.
She suggests combining it with the drip system.
qs.ev: which I’ll admit is the least exciting
qs.x: By calling her shed “the least exciting”, she concedes it is the least attractive option. She does not claim urgency or savings; Kwame is the one who says a box would be cheaper.

qs.q: How does Kwame interpret the city’s letter?
o: He thinks the cap was only for this summer.
He believes the letter was sent by mistake.
He suspects the garden’s water could be restricted further.
He expects the city to raise the garden’s allowance next year.
qs.ev: I read that as a warning
qs.x: He sees the planned review as a sign that the city could reduce or cut their water. It is Marguerite who thought the cap was a one-time thing.

qs.q: How does Kwame react to Ingrid’s comment about able-bodied gardeners?
o: He feels she has misrepresented his position.
He agrees that accessibility matters more.
He decides to withdraw his proposal.
He suggests she is exaggerating the costs.
qs.ev: That’s a bit unfair
qs.x: He objects that her comment is unfair and adds that he is not against the beds, so he feels his view was misrepresented. He keeps his proposal and later offers a cheaper version.

qs.q: What condition does Kwame attach to accepting the soaker hoses?
o: The installer must be booked before September.
The shed must be built next spring instead.
The group must reapply to the same neighbourhood fund in January.
The garden must begin harvesting rain from a nearby roof.
qs.ev: we start collecting rainwater from the community centre roof next spring
qs.x: His condition is collecting rainwater from the community centre roof. Reapplying in January is Ingrid’s idea for paying for barrels, not Kwame’s condition.

qs.q: What is Marguerite’s final position on the shed?
o: It should be bought with the remaining money.
She is willing to postpone it for now.
A storage box would be a poor substitute.
The neighbourhood fund should pay for it separately.
qs.ev: I’ll let the shed go, for this year at least
qs.x: “For this year at least” shows she is delaying the shed, not abandoning it. The remaining $600 goes to a storage box, not a shed.

qs.q: Why does Kwame plan to call the installer quickly?
o: The grant must be spent by mid-September.
The city will soon review its water allocation.
The installer cannot start new jobs for several weeks.
The price of the soaker hoses may go up in the fall.
qs.ev: He told me he’s fully booked until mid-September
qs.x: The installer is busy until mid-September, so booking early matters. The grant deadline is the end of October, not mid-September.

parts.context: A reporter presents different views on a town’s plan to buy and remove homes in a flood-prone neighbourhood.

lines: When the Saltmarsh River broke its banks in Belmont Flats last April, it was the third major flood in eleven years. This month, town council approved a plan that would once have been unthinkable: offering to buy all forty-seven homes in the lowest part of the neighbourhood, demolishing them, and letting the land return to floodplain. Supporters call it common sense. Critics call it giving up. The town’s chief engineer argues that the numbers speak for themselves. Since 2013, the town and the province have spent roughly nineteen million dollars on emergency response and repairs in Belmont Flats, and a proposed dike would cost another thirty million, with no guarantee it would hold against the kind of storms forecasters expect in the coming decades. By comparison, the buyouts are estimated at twenty-two million, paid once. In the engineer’s view, every dollar spent rebuilding in the same spot is a dollar spent preparing for the next disaster. But for many residents, the debate isn’t really about dollars. Doreen has lived on Ferry Lane for thirty-four years.

My husband built the back porch with his own hands. Our kids learned to swim in that river. I understand the flooding is getting worse, I’m not blind. But nobody asked us whether we wanted to be the town’s experiment. They held two public meetings, both on weekday afternoons, when most of my neighbours were at work.

Participation in the program is voluntary, at least for now. But residents who stay have been told that the town will no longer guarantee road maintenance or snow clearing once most homes are gone, which some say amounts to pressure. There’s also the question of price. The town is offering current market value, as assessed this year. An economist at the regional university who studies disaster recovery points out that market values in Belmont Flats have fallen sharply because of the floods themselves. In her words, “You’re paying people based on the very damage the town failed to prevent.” She doesn’t oppose buyouts, she says, but argues that fair compensation should be based on pre-flood values, or at least include moving costs, so families can afford comparable housing elsewhere in town.
If they offered me enough to buy something similar up the hill, I’d probably think about it. What they’re offering now wouldn’t buy a one-bedroom condo.

Meanwhile, environmental groups have praised the plan, noting that a restored wetland could absorb floodwater and protect neighbourhoods downstream. But some researchers caution that the benefits depend on how many owners actually sell. A patchwork of empty lots between occupied houses, they say, would bring little ecological benefit and leave the remaining residents more isolated than before. Council has set a deadline of next March for the first round of offers. Whether Belmont Flats becomes a model for other Canadian towns or a cautionary tale may depend on what happens between now and then.

o: The province has agreed to pay for most of the purchases.
A single payment costs less than repeated repairs and defences.

qs.x: He compares a one-time $22 million with $19 million already spent plus $30 million for a dike. The province helped pay for past repairs, but nothing says it will fund the buyouts.

qs.x: The meetings were at times when working residents were busy. She lives on Ferry Lane, but she never says invitations were limited to that street.

qs.x: Losing road maintenance and snow clearing makes staying difficult, so the choice may not feel free. March is the deadline for offers, not the date the program becomes mandatory.

qs.x: A patchwork of empty lots would bring little ecological benefit, so success depends on widespread selling. Environmental groups say the wetland would protect, not harm, downstream areas.

p1.meta: From: Nell Aubertin | To: Mateus Ferraz | Subject: My summer with the owls (and a big decision)
p1.text:
Hi Mateus,

I’m sorry it took me so long to reply to your message. You asked how my summer at the Cedar Hollow Wildlife Rescue went, and the honest answer is that it changed my mind about almost everything.

When I signed up in May, I expected to spend my Saturdays answering phones and maybe feeding a few baby birds. For the first month, that is more or less what happened. I cleaned cages, washed what felt like a thousand towels and learned to prepare food for animals I couldn’t even name. Then, in late June, one of the staff technicians broke her wrist, and suddenly they needed volunteers who could stay longer and help with actual patients. I ended up working three days a week in the clinic for the rest of the summer.

The highlight was a great horned owl that had been hit by a car near the highway. When she arrived, she couldn’t stand, and the vet wasn’t sure she would make it through the night. Seven weeks later, I watched her fly out of the release box and disappear into the trees behind the centre. I don’t think I’ve ever felt anything like it.

It wasn’t all wonderful, though. Not every animal makes it, and some of the decisions the staff have to make are heartbreaking. A few times I drove home and just sat in the car for twenty minutes before I could go inside.

Here’s the big news. The centre’s director has encouraged me to apply for the two-year wildlife technician diploma at the college in Brandon. Applications close on January 15, and classes start in September. The problem, of course, is money. I’d have to leave my job at the insurance office, and the starting salary for technicians is about two-thirds of what I earn now. Daniel thinks I should keep volunteering on weekends and see if I still feel the same in a year. Part of me knows he’s probably right, but another part worries that if I wait, I’ll talk myself out of it.

You went back to school at thirty-five, so I’d really value your opinion. Was it worth it?

Love,
Nell

Working several days a week in the clinic

qs.x: Answering phones and feeding baby birds are simple support jobs. Working in the clinic several days a week happened only later, after a technician was injured.

qs.ev: one of the staff technicians broke her wrist
qs.x: A technician broke her wrist, so the centre needed volunteers to help with patients. The director’s encouragement concerns the diploma, not the change in June.

qs.q: What does Nell suggest about the owl when it first arrived?
o: It had been injured by another animal.
It was too young to survive in the wild.
It needed surgery from a specialist vet.
Its chances of survival were uncertain.
qs.ev: the vet wasn’t sure she would make it through the night
qs.x: The vet doubted the owl would survive the night, so its survival was uncertain. It was hit by a car, not attacked by an animal, and no surgery is mentioned.

qs.q: Why does Nell mention sitting in her car?
o: To explain why she arrived home late so often
To show that the work could be emotionally draining
To suggest the drive to the centre was too long
To complain that the staff made poor decisions
qs.ev: A few times I drove home and just sat in the car for twenty minutes before I could go inside
qs.x: She needed time to recover after sad days, showing the emotional cost of the work. She calls the staff’s decisions heartbreaking, not poor.

qs.q: What is Nell’s main worry about the diploma?
o: She might not be accepted by the college.
Classes would begin before she was ready.
The program would take too long to complete.
Her income would fall if she changed careers.
qs.ev: the starting salary for technicians is about two-thirds of what I earn now
qs.x: She calls money “the problem”, since technicians earn about two-thirds of her current pay. The deadlines are simply facts; she never doubts she would be accepted.

qs.q: How does Nell feel about Daniel’s advice?
o: She sees its value but fears that waiting will weaken her resolve.
She rejects it because she has already decided to apply.
She agrees completely and plans to keep volunteering on weekends for now.
She thinks it shows he does not support her plans.
qs.ev: another part worries that if I wait, I’ll talk myself out of it
qs.x: She admits Daniel is “probably right” but worries delay will lead her to give up. She has not decided either way, which is why she asks Mateus for advice.

reply.intro: Here is Mateus’s response to Nell. Complete it by choosing the best option for each blank.
reply.text:
Hi Nell,

What a summer! I’m not surprised the centre noticed you – anyone who cheerfully tackles {1} clearly has the right attitude. I loved the story about the owl.

About the diploma: going back to school was the best decision I ever made, but I won’t pretend it was easy. I’d actually suggest a middle path between your instinct and Daniel’s advice. Since applications aren’t due until {2}, you have a few months to find out more. Could you ask the director whether the college offers {3}? Then you’d know if you could keep some income while you study. It’s also worth talking honestly with the technicians about the hard days, because the moments when you {4} won’t disappear once it’s your paid job.

Whatever you decide, don’t let the salary alone make the choice. Earning less doing work you love might be {5} than it sounds.

Hugs,
Mateus

p3.title: Living with Coyotes in the City
paras: Coyotes were once animals of the open prairie. A century ago, they were rarely seen east of Manitoba, but as forests were cleared for farms and wolves were driven out of much of their range, coyotes moved steadily eastward, reaching the Maritimes by the 1970s. Along the way, they proved remarkably flexible. A coyote will eat mice, rabbits, berries, insects, fallen fruit and, when it is available, garbage. That flexibility has carried them into the heart of Canadian cities, where they now live in ravines, golf courses, rail corridors and even cemeteries. Many residents are surprised to learn that coyotes have lived in their neighbourhoods for decades. Because the animals are mostly active between dusk and dawn, a family of coyotes can raise pups within a few hundred metres of a busy street without most people ever noticing them.

Much of what we know about urban coyotes comes from tracking studies, in which researchers fit animals with GPS collars and follow their movements for months. One such study in a large Prairie city followed thirty-two coyotes over three years. The findings were reassuring in some ways. Most of the animals went out of their way to avoid people, crossing roads late at night and resting during the day in thick brush. However, a small number behaved very differently. These coyotes spent more time near houses, approached people on paths and were seen in daylight far more often. When researchers examined their diets, they found a clear pattern: the bold animals were eating significantly more human food, whether from compost, bird feeders or deliberate handouts. In other words, the coyotes most likely to cause problems were the ones people had, knowingly or not, been feeding.

For pet owners, coyotes are a genuine concern, especially in late winter, when coyotes are breeding and defending territories, and in spring, when they are feeding pups. Small dogs left alone in yards and cats allowed to roam freely are at the greatest risk. Wildlife officers recommend keeping cats indoors, supervising small dogs and using a short leash on trails. If a coyote approaches, experts advise against running away. Instead, people should make themselves look large, wave their arms, shout and, if necessary, throw small objects in the animal’s direction. This practice, known as hazing, is meant to restore a coyote’s natural wariness of humans. It works best when a whole neighbourhood does it consistently; a coyote that is chased away by one household and fed by the next learns very little.

Municipal responses vary widely. For years, some communities responded to complaints by hiring trappers to remove coyotes. Biologists now generally regard this as ineffective. When coyotes are removed, the remaining animals often produce larger litters, and new coyotes quickly move into the empty territory, so populations recover within a year or two. Increasingly, cities are adopting coexistence plans instead. These typically combine public education, bylaws against feeding wildlife and a clear process for dealing with individual animals that become aggressive. One mid-sized Ontario city launched an online map last year where residents can report sightings, which staff use to identify hot spots and send outreach teams to specific streets. Officials there say the map has also revealed something unexpected: many reported “sightings” turned out to be foxes or large dogs.

qs.x: Paragraph B links bold behaviour to diets with more human food from compost, feeders or handouts.

qs.ev: the remaining animals often produce larger litters
qs.x: Paragraph D says removal leads the remaining coyotes to produce larger litters.

qs.x: City and prairie coyotes are both discussed, but no paragraph compares their lifespans.

qs.x: Paragraph A says coyotes moved east as wolves were driven out of much of their range.

qs.q: Scaring coyotes away has limited effect unless neighbours respond in the same way.

qs.x: Paragraph C says hazing works best when a whole neighbourhood does it consistently.

qs.q: The researchers who tracked coyotes recommended banning bird feeders in the city.
qs.x: Bird feeders are mentioned in B as a food source, but no recommendation or ban is reported anywhere.

qs.x: Paragraph A explains that coyotes active between dusk and dawn can live near busy streets unnoticed.

qs.x: Paragraph C names late winter and spring as periods of particular concern for pet owners.

p4.title: Our Parks Need Grass, Not Plastic
p4.byline: Opinion | by Corinne Vasquez, parks and environment columnist
p4.text:
Every spring, a familiar announcement appears on city websites across the country: another natural grass sports field is being replaced with artificial turf. The arguments in favour sound convincing. Turf fields can be used in the rain, they open weeks earlier in spring, and they don’t need mowing, fertilizer or watering. A single turf field, supporters say, can host as many games as three grass fields. For cities with long waiting lists for field time, that is an attractive promise.

But having spent the past year visiting parks and talking to groundskeepers, coaches and researchers, I have come to believe that the rush to plastic is a mistake – or at least a decision that is being made with only half the facts.

Start with heat. On a sunny July afternoon, the surface of an artificial field can reach sixty degrees Celsius or more, hot enough to blister skin. Grass fields in the same park rarely climb above thirty. As our summers grow hotter, we are building playing surfaces that become unusable precisely when children are out of school and most want to play. Several cities now spray water on their turf fields to cool them down, which rather undercuts the claim that turf saves water.

Then there is what happens to the fields over time. The plastic blades break down, and the rubber granules used as infill wash into storm drains and, eventually, into rivers and lakes. Most turf surfaces have to be replaced every eight to ten years, and recycling options for the old carpet remain limited. Much of it ends up in landfill or, worse, stockpiled in warehouses waiting for a solution that doesn’t yet exist.

The cost argument is also weaker than it first appears. A new turf field typically costs between one and two million dollars to install. Supporters point out that maintenance is cheaper than for grass, and that is true from year to year. But once you add the cost of replacing the surface every decade, the savings shrink considerably, and in some cases vanish altogether.

None of this means turf has no place. In a dense neighbourhood where one field must serve thousands of players, a turf surface may genuinely be the only way to meet demand. Indoor facilities and stadiums are a different question entirely. What I object to is turf becoming the default, rather than a carefully considered exception.

There is a better path for most fields. Modern natural grass fields built on a sand base with proper drainage can handle far more use than the soggy, clay-soaked fields many of us remember from childhood. They recover quickly after rain and, with good management, can be ready in spring only a week or two later than turf. They cost more to build than a typical grass field, but far less than turf, and they don’t need to be torn out and replaced.

Cities should commit to a simple rule: before any natural field is converted, staff must present a full comparison over twenty years, including replacement, disposal and heat impacts, alongside an upgraded grass option. Residents deserve to see the whole picture. If, after that, turf still makes sense, so be it. But I suspect that in most cases, it won’t.

qs.q: What is the writer’s main argument?
o: Cities should remove the turf fields they already have.
Turf should be chosen only after a full long-term comparison.
Turf is acceptable only inside stadiums and indoor facilities.
Grass fields should be watered less to reduce park costs.
qs.ev: What I object to is turf becoming the default, rather than a carefully considered exception
qs.x: She wants turf to be an exception chosen after a twenty-year comparison. She never calls for removing existing fields, and she says indoor facilities are a separate question.

qs.q: Why does the writer mention that some cities spray water on turf fields?
o: To explain how cities keep players safe in summer
To show that turf requires more staff than grass
To argue that turf fields should close in July
To question one of turf’s supposed advantages

qs.x: Watering turf to cool it weakens the claim that turf saves water. She does not present spraying as a safety solution or call for summer closures.

qs.q: What does the writer say about turf’s maintenance savings?

They are even greater than most supporters of turf usually admit.
They disappear entirely in every city that uses turf.
They are mainly the result of lower fertilizer costs.
qs.ev: once you add the cost of replacing the surface every decade, the savings shrink considerably
qs.x: She agrees maintenance is cheaper yearly but says replacement costs shrink the savings. She says they vanish only “in some cases”, not in every city.

qs.q: According to the writer, what is true of sand-based grass fields?
o: They can be used as early in spring as turf fields.
They cost less to build than a typical grass field.
They cost less than turf and do not need to be replaced.
They are best suited to dense urban neighbourhoods.
qs.ev: They cost more to build than a typical grass field, but far less than turf, and they don’t need to be torn out and replaced
qs.x: They cost far less than turf and never need replacing. They open a week or two later than turf, and they cost more than a typical grass field.

She believes residents there should be consulted first.
She worries that turf there is especially hot.
She accepts that it may be the only realistic option.

qs.x: She concedes turf may be the only way to meet heavy demand in dense areas. Consultation is part of her general proposal, not specific to crowded neighbourhoods.

t1.situation: You live in a 60-unit apartment building. For the past month, the shared recycling room has been overflowing: the bins are full days before collection, flattened and unflattened cardboard is piled on the floor, and you have seen signs of mice. Write an email to the property manager.
bullets: Describe the problem and how it is affecting residents
Explain what you think is causing it
Suggest two or three practical solutions
t1.model:
Dear Ms. Okafor-Reid,

I am writing about the recycling room on the ground floor, which has been overflowing for about a month. By Thursday each week, every bin is full, and residents have started leaving boxes and bags on the floor. Last weekend I noticed mouse droppings near the door, and several neighbours with small children have told me they no longer feel comfortable going in there.

I believe there are two main causes. First, many more residents now order groceries and household items online, so the amount of cardboard has increased dramatically. Second, a lot of boxes are being thrown in without being flattened, which means a single carton can fill half a bin.

I would like to suggest a few practical solutions. Could you ask the hauling company to add a second weekly pickup, or at least provide two additional bins? A simple sign asking people to flatten boxes, ideally with a pair of box cutters on a chain, would also help. Finally, a pest-control visit seems necessary before the problem gets worse.

Thank you for your attention. I would be happy to help put up notices.

Sincerely,
Andrés Villeneuve, Unit 512

t2.intro: The regional conservation authority is deciding how to manage Heron Creek Marsh, a wetland on the edge of your town. It can afford only one of the following options this year.
t2.question: Which option do you prefer?
t2.a: Build a 1.5-kilometre accessible boardwalk with viewing platforms and information signs, so that residents, school groups and people using wheelchairs can visit the marsh.
t2.b: Keep the marsh closed to visitors and spend the money on restoring habitat: removing invasive plants and creating protected nesting areas for endangered turtles and birds.
t2.model:
I would choose Option A, the accessible boardwalk, although I understand why the restoration project is appealing.

My main reason is that people protect what they know. At the moment, Heron Creek Marsh is little more than a name on a map for most residents. A boardwalk would allow families, seniors and school classes to see herons, turtles and frogs up close, and that kind of experience builds lasting public support for conservation. A raised boardwalk also keeps visitors on a single path, so the damage to plants and nesting areas should be minimal.

Secondly, accessibility matters. Many natural areas in our region are reached only by rough, muddy trails, which excludes people who use wheelchairs or walkers. A level boardwalk would be one of the few places where everyone can enjoy the outdoors.

Option B is certainly valuable, and I would not want the turtles forgotten. However, a closed marsh depends entirely on future funding decisions made by people who have never seen it. If the authority builds the boardwalk now, I believe residents will be far more willing to pay for restoration work in the years ahead.

t1.prompt: Your friend is planning their first solo three-day canoe trip in a provincial park this summer. They have canoed with groups before but have never travelled alone. Give your friend some advice about how to prepare and stay safe.
t1.model: First of all, I think it’s great that you’re doing this, but going solo is very different from paddling with a group, so I’d prepare carefully. The most important thing is to leave a detailed trip plan with someone you trust – your route, where you plan to camp each night and exactly when you expect to be back. Tell them who to call if they don’t hear from you by a certain time. I’d also seriously consider renting a satellite messenger, because there’s usually no cell signal in the backcountry. Second, choose a route you can manage comfortably. Maybe pick lakes with short portages and avoid big open water, because the wind can pick up really quickly in the afternoon, and a solo canoe is much harder to control. Try to paddle early in the morning and stay close to shore. Third, think about wildlife. Hang your food or use a bear barrel every single night, and cook well away from your tent. And finally, do a practice run. Load the canoe with all your gear and try a day trip close to home, so you know how it handles. If you prepare properly, I’m sure you’ll have an amazing time.

t2.prompt: Talk about a time when you were caught outdoors in bad or unexpected weather. What happened, and what did you learn from the experience?
t2.model: A few summers ago, my cousin and I went for a hike in the mountains. The forecast said sunny all day, so we only brought light jackets and a couple of sandwiches. About two hours in, the sky suddenly turned dark, and within ten minutes it was hailing – actual ice pellets the size of peas. We could hear thunder getting closer, and we were on an exposed ridge, which is the worst place to be. We ran down to a group of trees below the trail and crouched there, soaking wet and freezing, for almost forty minutes. When it finally cleared, we hiked back very slowly because the trail had turned into mud. I learned that mountain weather can change in minutes, no matter what the forecast says. Now I always pack a proper rain jacket, an extra layer and a plan for getting off high ground quickly.

scene.alt: A campsite beside a lake on a sunny summer day, with pine trees and a mountain in the background. On the left, a man in a dark blue shirt and a brown hat stands on the shore holding a fishing rod. Near him, a duck floats close to the water’s edge. In the centre, there is a green tent, and in front of it a small campfire is burning while a girl in a red shirt sits beside it. Out on the lake, a red canoe floats. On the right, a woman in a purple shirt with glasses reads a map at a picnic table, a woman in a teal shirt with long hair points toward the lake, and a black dog stands near them.

t3.prompt: Describe some things that are happening in the picture as well as you can. The person you are speaking to cannot see the picture.
t3.model: This picture shows a campsite beside a lake on a bright summer day. In the background there’s a mountain and some tall pine trees, and the sky is mostly clear. On the left, a man wearing a dark blue shirt and a brown hat is standing on the shore with a fishing rod, and there’s a duck floating just in front of him. In the middle, there’s a green tent, and right in front of it a small campfire is burning. A little girl in a red shirt is sitting beside the fire. Out on the water, there’s a red canoe, but I can’t see anyone in it. On the right, a woman with glasses is studying a map at a picnic table, while another woman in a teal shirt is pointing toward the lake. There’s also a black dog standing beside them.

t4.prompt: In this picture, what do you think will most probably happen next?
t4.model: I think the woman in the teal shirt is pointing at the empty canoe, and she’s probably just realized that it has drifted away from the shore. So most likely, she’ll call the others over, and the man with the fishing rod will put it down and try to reach the canoe – maybe he’ll wade into the water or use his rod to pull it closer. Meanwhile, the woman with the map will probably look up and join them, so the little girl might be left alone by the campfire for a moment. Hopefully one of the adults will remember to tell her to move back from the flames. The black dog will probably get excited by all the activity and might even jump into the lake after the canoe, which would make everything a lot more chaotic. In the end, I expect they’ll get the canoe back, tie it up properly and laugh about it over lunch.

t5.intro: Your workplace is planning its annual team day for September and has asked staff to vote on the activity. Choose the option that you prefer. In the next section, you will need to persuade a coworker that your choice is better than the one they prefer.

options.title: Volunteer trail-building day
details: Full day in a provincial park
Park bus picks the team up downtown
Physical work: digging and carrying gravel
Team name on a plaque on the new trail

options.title: Guided whitewater rafting trip
details: $95 per person, paid by the company
Everyone must be able to swim

other.title: Downtown cooking class
details: Cook and eat a three-course meal

t5.persuade: Your coworker prefers the downtown cooking class. Persuade your coworker that your choice is better.
t5.model: I know the cooking class is convenient, but I really think the trail-building day would be better for our team. First, it costs the company almost nothing, and it gives something back to the community. The park even sends a bus downtown, so getting there is just as easy as walking to the class. Second, think about what a team day is for. In a cooking class, we’d mostly stand at our own stations with the people we already talk to. On the trail, we’d have to work together, solve problems and share the heavy lifting, which is exactly the kind of teamwork we need. And it’s not just for the fit people – there are jobs for everyone. Finally, our names would be on a plaque on a trail we built. Years from now, we could take our families there. A three-course meal is nice, but we’d forget it by Monday.

t6.situation: You share a rented house with a roommate, and you split the utility bills equally. Since your roommate started working from home, they have been running two space heaters all day, and your share of the electricity bill has doubled to $190 a month. Your landlord has also mentioned in the past that the house’s old windows are very drafty.
options: Talk to your roommate and propose a different way of splitting the electricity bill.
Talk to your landlord and ask whether the drafty windows can be repaired or replaced.
t6.note: Choose ONE option and speak to that person.
t6.model: Hey Jordan, do you have a few minutes? I wanted to talk about the electricity bill, and I promise I’m not trying to start an argument. I totally understand why you use the space heaters – this house is freezing, especially your room by the old windows. The thing is, since you started working from home, my half of the bill has gone from about ninety-five dollars to a hundred and ninety, and that’s really hard for me on my budget. I was thinking we could split it based on usage instead. For example, we could compare this winter’s bills with last winter’s and divide the extra amount fairly. Or maybe you could pay sixty percent while you’re home all day. I’d also be happy to come with you to ask the landlord about the windows, because fixing the drafts would help both of us. What do you think would be fair?

t7.prompt: Some people believe that homeowners should be required to provide an official energy-efficiency rating for their home before it can be listed for sale, just as new appliances have energy labels. Others think this would add unnecessary cost and paperwork. What is your opinion? Explain your reasons.
t7.model: In my opinion, requiring an energy-efficiency rating before a home is sold is a good idea, and I have two main reasons. First, buying a home is the biggest purchase most people ever make, yet buyers usually know almost nothing about how much it will cost to heat or cool. When my friends bought their first house, they were shocked by a winter heating bill of over four hundred dollars a month, because the attic had almost no insulation. If they had seen a rating, they could have negotiated a lower price or budgeted for repairs. We already expect a label on a refrigerator, so it seems strange that a house has none. Second, a rating would encourage sellers to make improvements. If an efficient home sells faster or for a higher price, owners have a real reason to upgrade insulation or replace an old furnace, which also reduces emissions. I do understand the concern about cost. An assessment might cost a few hundred dollars, which could be hard for some sellers. However, that is a small amount compared to the price of a house, and the government could cover part of it for lower-income owners. Overall, I think the benefits clearly outweigh the inconvenience.

scene.alt: A lake on a sunny day with an enormous yellow rubber-duck-shaped duck floating in the middle of the water, taller than the pine trees nearby. A small orange canoe floats on the left beside it, looking tiny in comparison. On the shore, a man in a grey shirt is taking a photo with a camera, and a little boy in a green shirt is pointing at the giant duck. On the right, there is a white sign that says LAKE DAYS, a pine tree and a family of two small real ducks near the shore. A few clouds are in the sky.

t8.prompt: Your town is testing a giant floating duck on the lake as a possible attraction for its summer festival. You are on the shore and your friend, who is on the festival committee, calls you. Describe what you see and explain whether you think it should be part of the festival. Your friend cannot see the picture.
t8.model: Okay, I’m standing on the beach right now, and you won’t believe how big this thing is. Imagine a yellow duck, like a bath toy, but taller than the pine trees on the shore – I’d guess at least three storeys high. It’s floating right in the middle of the lake, and there’s a little orange canoe next to it that looks like a toy in comparison. People are already stopping to take photos, and a little boy beside me can’t stop pointing at it. There’s a sign that says Lake Days, and two real ducks near the shore that look pretty confused. Honestly, I think it should definitely be part of the festival. It’s fun, it’s easy to spot from the road, and everyone will share pictures online, which is free advertising. My only concern is safety for paddlers, so maybe we should keep canoes a few metres away from it.
